mcqs.question: Why does a web crawler design explicitly exclude ranking pages by relevance?
options: Ranking is a separate downstream system that consumes the crawler's stored pages, not part of what fetches and stores the corpus
Relevance ranking is technically impossible to implement at web scale
Crawlers never need to know anything about page content, only URLs
Robots.txt files forbid any ranking of crawled content
mcqs.explanation: Stating the ranking boundary keeps the design focused on the crawler's actual job: frontier, dedup, and politeness. Ranking is very much possible at scale (that's what search engines do) — it's just a different system built on top of the crawler's output. Crawlers do inspect content (for parsing links, fingerprinting duplicates); robots.txt has nothing to do with ranking.

mcqs.question: A crawler runs 10,000 requests/sec in aggregate across all domains. What does 'politeness' require of this traffic?
options: Reducing the total aggregate rate to under 1,000 requests/sec
Only crawling during off-peak hours for every domain
Capping the rate sent to any single domain, independent of the aggregate rate across all domains
Never crawling a domain more than once total
mcqs.explanation: Politeness is enforced per domain, not on the aggregate — a crawler can run enormous total throughput while still sending any individual site only one request every few seconds. There's no blanket aggregate cap, no universal off-peak rule, and re-crawling is expected (that's how freshness works), just paced per site.

mcqs.question: What is the practical consequence of a Bloom filter's false-positive rate in a crawler's URL-seen store?
options: The crawler might re-fetch some already-crawled pages unnecessarily
The crawler might treat a genuinely new URL as already-seen and silently skip crawling it
The crawler will crash when the false-positive rate is exceeded
The crawler will report a duplicate page as two separate pages in the index
mcqs.explanation: A Bloom filter false positive means it wrongly claims 'seen' for a URL that's actually new, so that page is silently never crawled. It never produces false negatives (it won't say 'not seen' for something already seen, so it won't cause re-fetches or duplicate-appearing pages from that mechanism), and there's no crash — it's a probabilistic trade-off, not a hard failure.

mcqs.question: The crawl team doubles the fetcher fleet but sees no increase in real page-fetch throughput. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The new fetchers are defective and need to be replaced
Per-domain politeness limits and DNS resolution are the real bottleneck, not fetcher count
The frontier needs to be rebuilt from scratch to recognize the new fetchers
Doubling fetchers always doubles throughput; something else in the pipeline must be broken
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic bottleneck trap: fetcher count stops mattering once per-domain rate limits and DNS lookups cap the effective throughput per domain. More fetchers just means more machines waiting on the same politeness clock. There's no fetcher defect and no frontier rebuild needed — and the assumption that doubling fetchers always doubles throughput is precisely what the scenario tests against.

mcqs.question: Why should re-crawl frequency be based on a page's observed change rate rather than a fixed interval for every page?
options: A fixed interval either lets fast-changing pages go stale or wastes fetch budget re-fetching pages that never change
Fixed intervals are technically impossible to implement in a distributed frontier
Observed change rate is required by most sites' robots.txt files
A fixed interval always exceeds the storage system's write capacity
mcqs.explanation: A uniform interval is a blunt instrument: it under-serves volatile pages (staying stale between crawls) and over-serves stable ones (wasting fetch budget). Adaptive re-crawl fixes both. Fixed intervals are perfectly implementable, robots.txt says nothing about crawl frequency, and storage capacity isn't the driver here.
